title: Pandas
description: Load, filter, group, join, and clean a real table.

lessons.title: The two objects everything else uses
lessons.lead: Pandas loads the first time you run a task here  give it a few seconds.

tasks.title: A labelled column
tasks.brief: Read one value out of the Series by its label, then print the mean, the labels that passed, and a count of the grades.
steps: The index labels each value, so `s["Sokha"]` works
`s[s >= 50].index.tolist()` gives the labels that passed
`.value_counts()` counts each grade  print it as a dictionary
starter: # 2. the mean, rounded to two places
# 3. the labels of everyone who scored 50 or more
# 4. how many of each grade, as a dictionary
tasks.hint: `float(s.mean())` before rounding keeps the printed value plain.
tasks.explain: A Series is a NumPy array plus an index. The boolean mask works exactly as it did in Module 03  what is new is that the labels travel with the values.

tasks.title: Look at a new table
tasks.brief: Print the shape, the column names, one column as a list, and prove which selections give a Series and which give a DataFrame.
steps: `df.shape` is `(rows, columns)`
`list(df.columns)` gives the labels
`type(x).__name__` prints the type name on its own
starter: # 3. the score column as a list
# 4. the type of df["score"] and of df[["name", "score"]]
tasks.hint: Print both type names on one line: `print(type(a).__name__, type(b).__name__)`.
tasks.explain: One column name gives a Series; a list of column names gives a DataFrame  even a list holding a single name.

lessons.title: Selecting rows and ordering them
lessons.lead: Build a boolean Series, hand it to `df[...]`, and assign through a single `.loc`.

tasks.title: Filter on one and two conditions
tasks.brief: Print the names who passed, the names who passed in class A, and then flag the failing rows with a new column.
steps: The pass mark is 50
Combine conditions with `&`, each in its own brackets
Assign the flag through `df.loc[rows, column]`
Fill the rows that were not flagged with `"ok"` before printing
starter: # 2. the names who passed and are in class A
# 3. set status to "retake" where the score is under 50,
#    then print the status column with the rest filled in as "ok"
tasks.hint: `df.loc[df["score"] < 50, "status"] = "retake"` creates the column and fills only the matching rows.
tasks.explain: Assigning through one `.loc` is the whole point  `df[df.score < 50]["status"] = "retake"` writes into a temporary copy and silently changes nothing.

tasks.title: Order the table
tasks.brief: Rank by score, then by class and score together, then take the top two and renumber the index.
steps: `ascending=False` puts the highest score first
Sorting on two columns takes a list of column names and a list of directions
`nlargest(2, "score")` is the shortcut for a top two
`reset_index(drop=True)` renumbers 0..n after sorting
starter: # 2. names by class ascending, then score descending
# 4. the index after sorting by score and resetting it
tasks.hint: `df.sort_values(["class", "score"], ascending=[True, False])` reads exactly as it sorts.
tasks.explain: Without `reset_index(drop=True)` the old row numbers travel with the sorted rows, so the index reads 3, 0, 2, 1  fine to keep, confusing to publish.

lessons.title: Split, apply, combine
lessons.lead: Group the rows by a column, summarise each group, and put the results back together as a table.

tasks.title: Average score per class
tasks.brief: Group by class and print the mean score, the number of students, and the top score in each group.
steps: `df.groupby("class")["score"].mean()` gives a Series indexed by class
Print each result as a dictionary with `.to_dict()`
Round the mean to two places first
starter: # 1. mean score per class, rounded to two places
tasks.hint: `.size()` counts the rows in each group; `.max()` works the same way as `.mean()`.
tasks.explain: The group labels become the index of the result. That is why `.to_dict()` reads as class to value with nothing extra.

tasks.title: Several summaries in one pass
tasks.brief: Use `.agg()` to build a small table with one row per class and three summary columns.
steps: Name each output column: `students=("name", "count")`
Call `.reset_index()` so the class labels become a normal column
Print the column names, then each column as a list
starter: # build a summary with students, avg_score and top_score per class
# 3. the average scores, rounded to two places
tasks.explain: This shape  one row per category, one column per measure  is what most reports and most charts want as their input.

lessons.title: Gaps and joins
lessons.lead: Two operations where a silent mistake changes your numbers without raising anything.

tasks.title: Count the gaps, then close them
tasks.brief: Report the missing values per column, drop the rows with no score, fill the missing class, and remove the duplicate id.
steps: `df.isna().sum()` counts the gaps  print it as a dictionary
A row with no score is useless, so drop those rows
Fill a missing class with `"unknown"`
Drop duplicate ids, keeping the first
starter: # 1. missing values per column, as a dictionary
# 2. drop the rows with no score, then print how many rows are left
# 3. fill the missing class with "unknown", then print the class column
# 4. drop duplicate ids, then print the ids that remain
tasks.hint: Work on one DataFrame the whole way through, reassigning it each step: `df = df.dropna(subset=["score"])`.
tasks.explain: Dropping and filling are both defensible; doing neither is not. Report which you chose for each column and why.

tasks.title: Three kinds of join
tasks.brief: Merge the two tables three ways and print how many rows each join returns, then the names that came back with no score.
steps: `how="inner"` keeps only the ids present on both sides
`how="left"` keeps every student
`how="outer"` keeps everything from both
After the left join, the missing score shows up as NaN
starter: # 1. row count of the inner join
# 2. row count of the left join
# 3. row count of the outer join
# 4. the names in the left join that have no score
tasks.hint: `merged[merged["score"].isna()]["name"].tolist()` picks out the rows the join could not fill.
tasks.explain: Id 4 has a score but no student, and id 3 has a student but no score. Which of them survives is entirely decided by `how`  always check the row count after a merge.
